passage:
Callum: Thermometer says the chicken's at 130°F. The recipe says it needs to hit 165°F.
Aiyana: I always pull mine at 120. It stays way juicier.
Callum: Okay, let's compromise and take it out at 145. Somewhere between the two has to be about right.
cue: Somewhere between the two has to be about right.
explanation: Callum picks 145°F only because it falls between the recipe and Aiyana's habit. A safe cooking temperature is a fact to look up, not a number to negotiate.

whyNot.fal_false_dichotomy: Callum isn't limiting the choices to two; he assumes the midpoint between two claims must be correct.

source: A dad at family movie night
passage: Okay, okay, both of you stop. Lena says the movie is rated for teens and up, Marcus says it's fine for everyone. I'm not looking it up again. Let's just say it's somewhere in the middle, like ten and up, so Marcus can watch the first half and we'll see how it goes.
cue: Let's just say it's somewhere in the middle, like ten and up
explanation: The movie's rating is a checkable fact, and one child is right. Dad settles on an in-between rating that nobody actually claimed, just because it splits the difference.

whyNot.fal_false_equivalence: Dad doesn't argue that the two claims are equally strong; he invents a rating halfway between them instead of checking.

source: Councillor Teodor Basu · Ashwyn council session
passage: I want to thank everyone who wrote in about the new signals on Kessler Avenue. Some residents tell me their commute has doubled. Our traffic engineer's data says travel times are down ten percent. My guess is reality sits between those two, which would mean the signals haven't changed much either way, so I see no reason to revisit them this year.
cue: My guess is reality sits between those two
explanation: Teodor has measured data and personal reports, but instead of weighing them he assumes the answer lies halfway and concludes the signals changed nothing.

whyNot.fal_false_dichotomy: Teodor isn't limiting the options to two; he takes two accounts and assumes the truth sits halfway between them.

passage: My DMs are split: half of you say kill the credit card first, half say max out retirement savings first. Both camps are so confident that the smart move must be doing a bit of each. So the plan is a 50/50 split of every extra dollar starting this month. (Card is at 24% APR, for anyone wondering.)
cue: Both camps are so confident that the smart move must be doing a bit of each
explanation: Tasha picks a 50/50 split because it sits between two confident camps, not because she compared them. With a 24% APR card, the numbers may clearly favor one side.

whyNot.fal_false_dichotomy: Tasha does consider a third option; her error is assuming the in-between one wins just because both sides sound sure.

title: Migration timeline for the board deck
passage: Hi Jonas, quick note on the timeline before Thursday. Our engineer, Sunil, estimates the database migration at six weeks, based on the last two we ran. The vendor's sales rep says it can be done in two. I've put four weeks in the deck, since reality usually lands somewhere between the optimistic and the cautious estimate. Let me know if that works. Renée
cue: reality usually lands somewhere between the optimistic and the cautious estimate
explanation: Renée's four weeks sounds prudent, but she picks it for being in the middle. Sunil's estimate rests on two past migrations; the sales rep's doesn't, and splitting them ignores that.

whyNot.fal_false_equivalence: Renée never declares the two estimates alike; her leap is choosing the midpoint without weighing which estimate is better supported.

title: Is the new diet-soda sweetener safe? Our columnist weighs in
passage: Two recent papers reach opposite conclusions about alluvose, the sweetener now in many diet sodas: one finds no effects at typical doses, the other reports headaches in a small trial. Columnist Hollis Mwangi's take: with researchers this divided, the sensible view is that it's mildly risky, so a can or two a week is probably fine.
cue: with researchers this divided, the sensible view is that it's mildly risky
explanation: Hollis lands on "mildly risky" because it sits between "no effects" and "causes headaches," not because any evidence points there. Weighing the two studies is the step he skips.

whyNot.fal_false_equivalence: Hollis's key leap isn't calling the two papers alike; it's concluding the truth must sit halfway between their findings.

title: Thermostat update
passage: Hi everyone, after the thermostat back-and-forth, we ran a two-week test at 71°F instead of 68 or 74. In the follow-up survey, 82% of you said you were comfortable, up from 41% before the test. Since the middle setting actually worked better for most people, we'll keep it at 71. Thanks for your patience! Gloria
cue: In the follow-up survey, 82% of you said you were comfortable, up from 41%
explanation: Gloria didn't pick 71°F just because it's in the middle. She tested it and kept it because the survey showed far more people were comfortable.

whyNot.fal_middle_ground: The compromise is justified by test results, not assumed to be right because it sits between two positions.

passage:
Abebe: The quote for the new fence is $1,800. I was hoping you'd cover it, since Biscuit knocked the old one down.
Wren: Fair, but that fence was 25 years old and already leaning, and the survey puts it exactly on our property line.
Abebe: True. It was due anyway and we both get the same fence, so $900 each seems fair.
cue: It was due anyway and we both get the same fence
explanation: Abebe agrees to split the cost for stated reasons: the old fence needed replacing regardless, and the new one sits on the line and benefits both yards equally.

whyNot.fal_middle_ground: The even split is backed by relevant facts about age and shared benefit, not chosen merely because it's halfway.
